paragraphs: November 12, 1996: Apple lays out a wild plan to get into the restaurant business, saying it will open a chain of Apple Cafes with a touchscreen point-of-sale system. The company envisioned themed establishments where diners could eat, surf the web and even videoconference with people at other tables

A bit like the company’s future retail stores — but without the computers and iPhones for sale — the Apple restaurants would open in cities around the world. The first, Apple says, will be a 15,000-square-foot restaurant in Los Angeles, opening in late 1997.

Before Apple Stores became synonymous with chic shopping and carefully controlled customer experiences, Cupertino nearly tried something much stranger: a worldwide chain of high-tech restaurants. It was a wildly ambitious attempt to turn Apple’s brand into a lifestyle destination.

But the company was flailing, and the restaurant dream became another casualty of Apple’s anything-goes era. When Steve Jobs returned the following year, he had a very different idea about where Apple’s future should be — and it didn’t involve serving lunch.

Still, the Apple Cafes almost became a thing. Apple partnered with London company Mega Bytes International BVI for the ill-fated restaurant endeavor. The idea was, essentially, to establish a chain of high-profile cybercafes. The concept held a lot of appeal at a time when only 23% of U.S. residents enjoyed the internet at home. (Today, that figure stands at more than 94%, according to Statista.)

Plus, theme restaurants like Planet Hollywood were going gangbusters in the 1990s. The concept of hooking up with a tech company — albeit an ailing one — to sell food seemed as serious as many business plans in the early dot-com era.

The retro-styled Apple Cafes would boast seating for approximately 250 patrons. Customers would take advantage of internet connections, CD-ROM access and FaceTime-style videoconferencing with other diners. Small shops within the restaurants would sell Apple merchandise and software. Alongside Los Angeles, Apple scouted potential locations in London, Paris, New York, Tokyo and Sydney.
The Apple Cafe plan sounds like a wacky idea now. However, the idea of a computer company running a restaurant chain isn’t quite as obviously doomed as it might sound.
